analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from enforcing non-compete agreements against hourly and other non-exempt workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have voided existing non-competes and banned new ones for non-exempt employees, was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on August 30, 2022, received no cosponsors, and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal wage law to make non-compete agreements unenforceable against workers who are covered by federal overtime rules — generally hourly and lower-paid employees. It would void every existing non-compete with such workers, ban employers from writing new ones, and let courts impose penalties on employers who try to enforce them. Employers could still require employees to keep trade secrets confidential. The bill was introduced near the end of the 117th Congress, sent to committee, and never taken up; it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, non-exempt employees — broadly, hourly and lower-paid workers covered by federal overtime rules — would gain the freedom to leave a job for a competitor without fearing a lawsuit, which typically means better wages and more bargaining power. New job seekers and workers relocating geographically would also benefit, since existing non-competes would be void.

how_it_helps.text: It voids existing non-competes and bars employers from entering, extending, or renewing them for non-exempt workers, letting those employees change jobs freely.
It forbids employers from even threatening to enforce a non-compete, and creates penalties under the Fair Labor Standards Act enforceable in court.
It preserves employers' ability to protect trade secrets through confidentiality agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on non-competes to retain lower-paid staff — including staffing firms, franchises, and service companies — would lose a tool for keeping wages down and workers from leaving, and could face federal penalties for enforcing such agreements.

drawbacks.text: The ban does not apply to employees exempt from federal overtime rules — generally salaried professionals and managers — so those workers could still be bound by non-competes.
The exemption covers salaried professional, executive, and administrative employees, but not the lowest-paid workers.
Voiding existing agreements retroactively could create legal uncertainty for disputes already underway, though the bill applies only to proceedings commenced after its effective date.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to non-exempt workers is real and substantial: non-competes hold back wages and job mobility even for lower-paid employees. But the bill as written had a notable carve-out — exempt (typically salaried) employees would remain bound — and voiding existing agreements could produce litigation over disputes filed after the effective date. Supporters would acknowledge the exemption weakens the policy; opponents would argue a blanket federal ban interferes with contractual freedom. On the whole, for the workers it covered, the benefits outweighed the costs, which is why its total inaction is the real loss.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced, dying there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 30, 2022, near the end of the 117th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, where no markup or vote ever occurred.
It attracted zero cosponsors, including none from the sponsor's own party.
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, so the bill died without any floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who use non-competes to hold hourly and lower-paid workers in place are better off; those workers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Mike Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 30, 2022 and recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up, but controlled what the committee and chamber took up; its death in committee reflects the leadership's priorities.

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded vote and no cosponsor of either party, so partisan positions never became visible; the only recorded actor was the Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Employers that use non-competes (staffing agencies, service franchises, healthcare, tech)
industries.note: Non-competes help such firms hold workers in place and depress wage competition; the bill would void and ban them for non-exempt staff.
Any business relying on non-competes to keep lower-paid workers from leaving would lose that tool; workers would gain bargaining power.
